Interviewer:	The project that we're working on is looking at women in engineering and we've decided to include design and technology students in that as well, for two reasons really: one because we are also working with [name] University, and the design and technology side falls under engineering there (right) and then we're kind of looking at engineering as a male dominated environment, so we're looking at design and technology, to see if it's the same, that's the context and we're also looking at women's experiences of education so far and why they want to do a placement and what they're expecting to get out of placement and are you doing the placement?

Subject:	No I'm not.

Interviewer:	And also if you're not doing the placement, why some students chose not to do the placement. So I'll start off by asking a few background questions, if that's OK with you and how you started, became interested in engineering – that sort of thing. What A levels did you do?

Subject:	I did physics, photography (or geography?), design technology and media.

Interviewer:	OK, what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Er, I went to the local comprehensive school.

Interviewer:	Not an all girls' school or anything like that?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	OK. Have you got any previous work experience in engineering?

Subject:	Not really no.

Interviewer:	OK, what do your parents do, are either of them involved in the industry at all?

Subject:	No, my brother is – my brother's doing the same thing but my parents aren't. My dad's more of a manager.

Interviewer:	Is he? So when and why do you think that you decided to do design & technology?

Subject:	Erm, it was always one of my better subjects at school, that I actually enjoyed – I got good marks on, that's why I carried on.

Interviewer:	OK, what sort of things appealed to you about it when you were at school?

Subject:	I think probably because it's more sort of – I think, I have – I think it's just the creativity – like, that you can do, you're not just stuck at you know, sort of writing an essay you had to get to you know – there are several aspects, you're not just stuck doing one thing. You get to do model making, you can go and do rendering, there's loads of things you can actually do.

Interviewer:	OK, yeah, that's fine. Do you think it encouraged you, the thought that your brother was doing a similar course?

Subject:	Erm, I think it helped yeah, because erm my family have always been sort of Art & Design, sort of like you know, with my parents, we went round galleries and things like that and to see exhibitions and stuff, so I think that's probably encouraged me a bit.

Interviewer:	OK, did you do much career research or did you have any careers advice and stuff while you were at school?

Subject:	No, I mean my technology teacher did the same thing and actually came to [this university] and he talked to me a bit about the background and what it was like but other than that, not really. I mean I did things like the work – the work experience at school but that was like in an office for like a couple of days. Erm, so I had that sort of view on it but that it was it really.

Interviewer:	OK, so how did you decide to come to [this] University?

Subject:	Er, because – well, I was told it was supposed to be the best university for this course. That's why. There were several universities and I think [university] had the highest points, that's why I put [university] first. Because of it's like reputation, because I thought well, you know, obviously aim for the highest one, if not then go for one with lower points.

Interviewer:	OK, that's fine. Did you realise that design & technology was so male dominated?

Subject:	Er, yeah. I did from 'A' level, when I was about the only girl in the class. So I knew from experience that it was.

Interviewer:	Did it bother you at all?

Subject:	Not really, no. I didn't mind.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that more women should be encouraged to do design & technology?

Subject:	I think so, yeah.

Interviewer:	Why do you think the reason is they don't do it?

Subject:	I think it's just the association of how girls see it – you know – dominated by males and I think that at times some of the – just the association – you know, there are things I have to do like (?) students have to do the model making and doing the workshop. It's sort of – it's erm, they probably might not see what you do. You know, it does tend to be like most of the staff tend to be male and it does have that sort of relationship, you know, you're DIY seems to be sort of male orientated.

Interviewer:	Have you got any ideas or thoughts on what could be done to encourage more women to take it up?

Subject:	Erm, I don't know really.

Interviewer:	Do you think it would have helped you if you'd had more information about – like you said it's associated with being male – do you think that it's probably people's perceptions that might be false perceptions?

Subject:	Yeah, I think a lot of the examples you see, tend to be sort of male examples, so it probably would be better if you know, you had more reference to females in it, their sort of side of it

Interviewer:	OK, what characteristics do you think make a good designer?

Subject:	Er, you need determination, erm, er, you need to be creative, you need to be committed to it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that men or women are better at any of those things?

Subject:	Erm, I think well, in my opinion, they mainly seem to be male sort of natural, you know when they're sort of sketching away they seem more natural – whereas I think that girls tend to sort of put more effort into and girls are probably a lot more organised and probably more structured. But I don't think there's anything really specific that I'd say more than the other.

Interviewer:	OK, that's fine. Do you think that there are any advantages to being a woman in like a male dominated environment?

Subject:	You do – well not so much here but when I was school I did tend to get more help, because I was the only girl and all the lads tended to stick together. There's that but then I don't think there is here.

Interviewer:	Did you find that that was really an advantage, did it annoy you at all or were you happy?

Subject:	Well I found it, if I wanted to get on with my work and not be bothered then, I was left alone, sort of thing, but then again it was useful to sort of have that bit of extra help.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that there are any disadvantages to being a woman?

Subject:	I think it's a disadvantage that people don't take you seriously enough. They do sort of think that, oh you know, why should – you know, it – I think the workshop's probably the best example, where it's like, oh no you're a woman you shouldn't be doing that kind of thing.

Interviewer:	And do you find that you have experiences of that happening?

Subject:	Er, not really no. Like personally I haven't but I have heard people that – you know – some other people, but personally I haven't

Interviewer:	OK. Has the course been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	Yes and no. I expected a lot of course work and a lot of work, er but there are some things – I think it's just because I didn't – you know that I never covered them at school, so therefore I didn't – you know – obviously there was a (?) and sort of like girls from school to industry and it was just sort of, you know, you kind of weren't aware that we'd be covering them in like as much depth.

Interviewer:	OK what would you say are the best and the worst things about the course?

Subject:	Erm, the worst thing I would say is having too much work all at once (yeah) but the best things are that I do actually enjoy the work. Like you know, when I sit down to do it, it is something that I enjoy doing. I think really, at times they have people in – that have been in industry, you know, they're in for like a couple of weeks or whatever and it's good, as well, to have that influence as well as just lecturers.

Interviewer:	OK. That's great. Have you been taught by any female lecturers at all?

Subject:	Yes, but she's now left.

Interviewer:	OK, would you find it encouraging if you had more female lecturers?

Subject:	Yeah. It would be, 'cos at the moment there's all male. It would be yeah.

Interviewer:	What do you think would be the advantages of having a female?

Subject:	I think it's just a different view that they give on the old work like. Erm, it's not just getting one opinion from, you know, it's obvious if you go to see somebody about your work – it's all male, so you know, obviously there is some things what you need a female sort of view like. I think that would be helpful.

Interviewer:	OK, did you think that female lecturers treat you the same as the male lecturers?

Subject:	Er, they – they teach – they taught differently.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do you think that was a gender thing or do you think it was down to individuals?

Subject:	I think it might have been down to individuals. Because I've only been taught by one female lecturer it's hard to say because it's just basing it on that one person.

Interviewer:	OK, what about the male lecturers, do they treat female students the same?

Subject:	They do yes, but now and then they'll make like – you know – obviously female jokes but erm I wouldn't say they necessarily sort of treat you differently on purpose.

Interviewer:	Do you find they generally make jokes or…?

Subject:	Well it's normally quite annoying because it's just one female – there's no females there to do the same the same to the blokes, so I don't know. I don't know, I think there's always going to be those kinds of jokes in society.

Interviewer:	Have you got a personal tutor?

Subject:	Yeah I have.

Interviewer:	Are they male as well? Would you prefer a female or aren't you really bothered?

Subject:	No, I don't mind but er I've got a really good tutor so I'm quite happy. I'm just happy I've got like a good tutor.

Interviewer:	OK, that's great. Is there anything or anyone that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

Subject:	Erm, probably not no.

Interviewer:	OK. Have you had to do much group work?

Subject:	We've done a bit, yes. 

Interviewer:	Do you like doing group work?

Subject:	I do like doing group work – but at times it has been a bad experience.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Have you got any examples of when it's been bad?

Subject:	Well the – one of the group projects we had to do last semester we were a group of 5 and you know, one of the lads was just really annoying and he tended to object to a lot of things. He wasn't really – he wasn't a group sort of person, you know? Whereas we'd sit down and go through, he'd take – you know, he preferred to go off by himself.

Interviewer:	OK, do you prefer to work with men or women in groups or ..?

Subject:	I have no preference. I mean I've experienced both and as long as it's somebody you get on well with and work together with, I don't mind.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

Subject:	Yeah, I think they do because erm another group project that I had last semester, it was me working with two guys and erm, the stuff that I'd done, the stuff that I sort of brought to the work was different to what you know, they'd done, so that was probably useful because we were able to get a broader range of everything.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that it's good to do group work, in the sense of the skills that you get from it?

Subject:	I think it is yeah, because also next time when you come to do something on your own, you may think oh well they thought of that and I didn't, therefore I'll make sure I do it as if they – you know you remember things from what you've learnt and you just pick it up.

Interviewer:	Do you think it helps you when you finish university as well?

Subject:	I think it does. Well yeah, I mean obviously if I go into a job where you have to keep you know – you have to be able to communicate with other people.

Interviewer:	OK, why did you decide not to go on a placement?

Subject:	I think it's more of my style of study – if I take a year out, I don't know if I'd – I'd find it really difficult to get back into the flow of working again, 'cos after the length of the summer holiday I find it really difficult getting back into the flow of like you know having to deal with a lot of course work and that. So that's really what it is. I just don't want to get out of the uni system.

Interviewer:	Yeah, absolutely. Do you think that there would have been any advantages to doing a placement?

Subject:	Er, not from what I've seen – like people that I know that have done placements and they're still struggling to find jobs. But I think it obviously depends on if you – if you're settled on placement and you know, they might offer you a job afterwards but from the people I've seen it's been a struggle for them whether they've had a placement or not.

Interviewer:	OK, do you know the type of company that you'd like to work for when you finish?

Subject:	No, I haven't got a clue.

Interviewer:	OK, so what sort of thing do you think will attract you to a company? Will it be the type of work that you do or things like money and location or training opportunities – anything like that?

Subject:	I think it will be the type of work that I'm going to do. Obviously I want a well paid job. Location – I'm not really too bothered about and training opportunities I think, to begin with I wouldn't mind if there weren't any training opportunities but then after, you know after a while, I'll be able to see what options there are.

Interviewer:	Yeah, OK. How do you think that work will be different from being at University?

Subject:	Er, I think you'll be focussed more on one aspect. You won't be doing you know – you won't be asked to do everything for this one – well, erm whatever they're working on I suppose. Obviously, I think a job's going to be much more working in teams, so that's why.

Interviewer:	Do you think how you're treated will be the same?

Subject:	Not really no. I think it will really be when you've gained a lot of experience, that you know – you won't just be the person who's left uni, you'll actually have your own experience.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that there's anything that you will take, from the course, that will help you when you start work? Like the skills that you've learnt or any advice that you've had?

Subject:	I think we'd have to apply the skills that we've learnt. I'm not quite – I think also I don't think I'll have to use all of them, it'll just be in specific areas and advice, I don't think so – I mean, 'cos other people have tried to indicate what it's actually like but I don't think you can – you can really know until you do it yourself. So you know, then obviously each working situation's different, so …

Interviewer:	So do you think that university could do anything to help prepare you for going out to work or are there so many different directions that you could go, it's too difficult?

Subject:	Yeah. I mean there's so many directions and because everybody works differently you know, what might be relevant to one person isn't going to be to another.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think will be the best and worst things about when you start work?

Subject:	I think the best things will be you've got – you know, like you finish for the day we might not have to – you know, you don't necessarily have to take it home with you. So, you know, I hope that you know you will have to work longer hours – it's fixed but you're like working Monday to Fridays and the weekends are yours and you don't have to think oh I've got to get this finished for Monday – I've got that to do. I think that's gonna be a good side. The bad thing hmm, I don't know, just the fact that you actually have to be at a desk for 9 O'clock.

Interviewer:	OK, in terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in say 5 years time?

Subject:	Erm, I don't know. Hopefully I will have been working for a company for several years. And I want to think about how I can further myself.

Interviewer:	What sort of things is it that you'd like to do or…do you think you'll go into like management or become more specialised or stuff?

Subject:	I think I'll probably prefer to go into more management and I'll be required to do a bit of further training and then you know, start that up and gradually work my way up the ladder.

Interviewer:	OK, what then would be your ideal career?

Subject:	Sorry?

Interviewer:	What would be your ideal career?

Subject:	My ideal career? Erm, well I think it's photography, which isn't actually what I'm doing, but yeah, I think photography. But because obviously, it's so difficult to get into and also there aren't many decent photography jobs available that's why I did design.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that you'll go into the design industry then?

Subject:	I think I will but I'm not sure if it's – you know – which form to go into. I think I will go into the design industry but I don't have a lot of set thing of, oh you know, I want to work here, I want to do that because I haven't decided on that yet.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that the career prospects are good in design and technology?

Subject:	I think so. I mean it's like any, you know, any job where every now and then its is not going to be – you know – (many places?) well I think, because obviously technology is advancing – there's so many products on the market, that you know if you can basically design anything, as long as there's a need for it.

Interviewer:	Yeah. What about once you get in the industry, what are the prospects like for developing your career?

Subject:	I think there's only so far you can go then once you get to the top obviously it's just sort of you're the one with the designs that everybody wants. So I don't know. There is a – definitely several steps you can get to get higher up and go into management, but I think there is a limit on it.

Interviewer:	OK, are you happy with all the career choices you've made so far, or do you wish you'd done anything differently at all?

Subject:	In a way, perhaps I wish I'd done something else but then there's nothing else that I would really want to do (yeah) so yeah and plus, I do actually enjoy the work that we do – that's one thing I've found with it.

Interviewer:	OK, what 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics of design and technology?

Subject:	Er, 5 words? Erm, (long pause) I don't know.

Interviewer:	That's OK. Do you think that it is masculine?

Subject:	Er, yes, I think it is.

Interviewer:	Do you think that's purely to do with the numbers of men involved in the industry?

Subject:	I think it is. I think it's because of all the males and also a lot of erm, a lot of famous companies that you see – sort of at the head of it is a male, so I think that's probably – I think so, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the situation will get better?

Subject:	I think so because it seems to be that you do see erm well you do see, when the interviews have been happening – there's definitely more and more girls there compared to when I've been at some places where I was interviewed.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that any aspects of the culture will be problematic for you in work? Do you think the fact that it's so male dominated will cause any problems for you?

Subject:	I shouldn't think so, no. I think you know, if you go for an interview, it may be that, you know, there's like 5 males to 1 female – that goes for the job, but at the same time it's based on you know, your portfolio and you know, you as a person rather than if you're male or female.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that your educational experiences differ from other students that have been in say social subjects, like humanities – something like that?

Subject:	I think yeah, definitely. It does seem that we put more time and effort into it and also a lot of the people that, you know, it's sort of, oh if they miss a lecture, it doesn't matter, or if they're late coming in. We don't have that you know, if we miss a lecture we're mainly fail on something, you know, we needed to know. You know, a skill that's been taught so it's sort of – the fact that we have to go to lectures and you actually have to sit and I do seem to be doing a lot more course work than my other friends.

Interviewer:	Do you think that's a good or a bad thing?

Subject:	I think – for being at university, for me, it's a bad thing, 'cos it's like what a one off chance to be at university, and you want to try everything but then it's also good because in – you know, when you come to be in industry, you're obviously going to have to put in a lot of work.

Interviewer:	OK that's everything, thank you.

Erm, it's not just getting one opinion from, you know, it's obvious if you go to see somebody about your work – it's all male, so you know, obviously there is some things what you need a female sort of view like. I think that would be helpful.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you think that female lecturers treat you the same as the male lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, they – they teach – they taught differently.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Do you think that was a gender thing or do you think it was down to individuals?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it might have been down to individuals. Because I've only been taught by one female lecturer it's hard to say because it's just basing it on that one person.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what about the male lecturers, do they treat female students the same?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They do yes, but now and then they'll make like – you know – obviously female jokes but erm I wouldn't say they necessarily sort of treat you differently on purpose.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you find they generally make jokes or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well it's normally quite annoying because it's just one female – there's no females there to do the same the same to the blokes, so I don't know. I don't know, I think there's always going to be those kinds of jokes in society.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you got a personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah I have.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are they male as well? Would you prefer a female or aren't you really bothered?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I don't mind but er I've got a really good tutor so I'm quite happy. I'm just happy I've got like a good tutor.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that's great. Is there anything or anyone that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, probably not no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Have you had to do much group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We've done a bit, yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you like doing group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I do like doing group work – but at times it has been a bad experience.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Have you got any examples of when it's been bad?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well the – one of the group projects we had to do last semester we were a group of 5 and you know, one of the lads was just really annoying and he tended to object to a lot of things. He wasn't really – he wasn't a group sort of person, you know? Whereas we'd sit down and go through, he'd take – you know, he preferred to go off by himself.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you prefer to work with men or women in groups or ..?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I have no preference. I mean I've experienced both and as long as it's somebody you get on well with and work together with, I don't mind.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think they do because erm another group project that I had last semester, it was me working with two guys and erm, the stuff that I'd done, the stuff that I sort of brought to the work was different to what you know, they'd done, so that was probably useful because we were able to get a broader range of everything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that it's good to do group work, in the sense of the skills that you get from it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it is yeah, because also next time when you come to do something on your own, you may think oh well they thought of that and I didn't, therefore I'll make sure I do it as if they – you know you remember things from what you've learnt and you just pick it up.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it helps you when you finish university as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it does. Well yeah, I mean obviously if I go into a job where you have to keep you know – you have to be able to communicate with other people.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, why did you decide not to go on a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it's more of my style of study – if I take a year out, I don't know if I'd – I'd find it really difficult to get back into the flow of working again, 'cos after the length of the summer holiday I find it really difficult getting back into the flow of like you know having to deal with a lot of course work and that. So that's really what it is. I just don't want to get out of the uni system.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, absolutely. Do you think that there would have been any advantages to doing a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, not from what I've seen – like people that I know that have done placements and they're still struggling to find jobs. But I think it obviously depends on if you – if you're settled on placement and you know, they might offer you a job afterwards but from the people I've seen it's been a struggle for them whether they've had a placement or not.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you know the type of company that you'd like to work for when you finish?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I haven't got a clue.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, so what sort of thing do you think will attract you to a company? Will it be the type of work that you do or things like money and location or training opportunities – anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it will be the type of work that I'm going to do. Obviously I want a well paid job. Location – I'm not really too bothered about and training opportunities I think, to begin with I wouldn't mind if there weren't any training opportunities but then after, you know after a while, I'll be able to see what options there are.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, OK. How do you think that work will be different from being at University?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I think you'll be focussed more on one aspect. You won't be doing you know – you won't be asked to do everything for this one – well, erm whatever they're working on I suppose. Obviously, I think a job's going to be much more working in teams, so that's why.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think how you're treated will be the same?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really no. I think it will really be when you've gained a lot of experience, that you know – you won't just be the person who's left uni, you'll actually have your own experience.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that there's anything that you will take, from the course, that will help you when you start work? Like the skills that you've learnt or any advice that you've had?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think we'd have to apply the skills that we've learnt. I'm not quite – I think also I don't think I'll have to use all of them, it'll just be in specific areas and advice, I don't think so – I mean, 'cos other people have tried to indicate what it's actually like but I don't think you can – you can really know until you do it yourself. So you know, then obviously each working situation's different, so …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So do you think that university could do anything to help prepare you for going out to work or are there so many different directions that you could go, it's too difficult?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I mean there's so many directions and because everybody works differently you know, what might be relevant to one person isn't going to be to another.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think will be the best and worst things about when you start work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think the best things will be you've got – you know, like you finish for the day we might not have to – you know, you don't necessarily have to take it home with you. So, you know, I hope that you know you will have to work longer hours – it's fixed but you're like working Monday to Fridays and the weekends are yours and you don't have to think oh I've got to get this finished for Monday – I've got that to do. I think that's gonna be a good side. The bad thing hmm, I don't know, just the fact that you actually have to be at a desk for 9 O'clock.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, in terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in say 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don't know. Hopefully I will have been working for a company for several years. And I want to think about how I can further myself.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What sort of things is it that you'd like to do or…do you think you'll go into like management or become more specialised or stuff?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think I'll probably prefer to go into more management and I'll be required to do a bit of further training and then you know, start that up and gradually work my way up the ladder.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what then would be your ideal career?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Sorry?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What would be your ideal career?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: My ideal career? Erm, well I think it's photography, which isn't actually what I'm doing, but yeah, I think photography. But because obviously, it's so difficult to get into and also there aren't many decent photography jobs available that's why I did design.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that you'll go into the design industry then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think I will but I'm not sure if it's – you know – which form to go into. I think I will go into the design industry but I don't have a lot of set thing of, oh you know, I want to work here, I want to do that because I haven't decided on that yet.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that the career prospects are good in design and technology?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so. I mean it's like any, you know, any job where every now and then its is not going to be – you know – (many places?) well I think, because obviously technology is advancing – there's so many products on the market, that you know if you can basically design anything, as long as there's a need for it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. What about once you get in the industry, what are the prospects like for developing your career?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think there's only so far you can go then once you get to the top obviously it's just sort of you're the one with the designs that everybody wants. So I don't know. There is a – definitely several steps you can get to get higher up and go into management, but I think there is a limit on it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you happy with all the career choices you've made so far, or do you wish you'd done anything differently at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In a way, perhaps I wish I'd done something else but then there's nothing else that I would really want to do (yeah) so yeah and plus, I do actually enjoy the work that we do – that's one thing I've found with it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics of design and technology?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, 5 words? Erm, (long pause) I don't know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That's OK. Do you think that it is masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yes, I think it is.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that's purely to do with the numbers of men involved in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it is. I think it's because of all the males and also a lot of erm, a lot of famous companies that you see – sort of at the head of it is a male, so I think that's probably – I think so, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the situation will get better?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so because it seems to be that you do see erm well you do see, when the interviews have been happening – there's definitely more and more girls there compared to when I've been at some places where I was interviewed.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that any aspects of the culture will be problematic for you in work? Do you think the fact that it's so male dominated will cause any problems for you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I shouldn't think so, no. I think you know, if you go for an interview, it may be that, you know, there's like 5 males to 1 female – that goes for the job, but at the same time it's based on you know, your portfolio and you know, you as a person rather than if you're male or female.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that your educational experiences differ from other students that have been in say social subjects, like humanities – something like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think yeah, definitely. It does seem that we put more time and effort into it and also a lot of the people that, you know, it's sort of, oh if they miss a lecture, it doesn't matter, or if they're late coming in. We don't have that you know, if we miss a lecture we're mainly fail on something, you know, we needed to know. You know, a skill that's been taught so it's sort of – the fact that we have to go to lectures and you actually have to sit and I do seem to be doing a lot more course work than my other friends.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that's a good or a bad thing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think – for being at university, for me, it's a bad thing, 'cos it's like what a one off chance to be at university, and you want to try everything but then it's also good because in – you know, when you come to be in industry, you're obviously going to have to put in a lot of work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK that's everything, thank you.
